# Anti-assignment clauses; change of control; asset sales

*Citation:* *SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §317, §322; Texas cases on 'operation of law'  
*Status in this library:* in force

A clause barring assignment 'by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise' is enforced according to its terms; an asset sale transferring the contract without consent is a breach and the transfer is void where the clause so provides. Absent such language, assignment of contract rights is generally permitted; obligations require consent only if performance is personal. A consent requirement that may be withheld 'in sole discretion' gives the counterparty leverage to renegotiate price.

--- baskets_caps.md ---
# Indemnity baskets and caps — deductible vs tipping; survival

*Citation:* ABA Deal Points Study (private targets); market summary  
*Status in this library:* in force

A **deductible** basket: seller pays only losses above the threshold. A **tipping** basket: once the threshold is crossed, seller pays from the first dollar. Market: cap ~10% of price for general reps; fundamental reps and taxes to purchase price; **a specific operational rep (like worker classification) carved out to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with a sized special indemnity**. Survival 12–24 months general.

--- earnout_definitions.md ---
# Earn-out drafting — EBITDA definitions and buyer control

*Citation:* Practice note; *Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015)  
*Status in this library:* in force

An earn-out measured by 'EBITDA as determined by Buyer under Buyer's policies' lets the buyer allocate overhead, management fees, integration costs and purchase-accounting adjustments against the target, zeroing the earn-out. Seller protections: defined accounting principles (seller's historical practices or GAAP consistently applied), exclusion of buyer overhead allocations and transaction/integration costs, covenant to operate the business in the ordinary course and not take actions with the purpose of avoiding the earn-out, information and audit rights, dispute resolution by an independent accountant, acceleration on sale of the business.

--- sandbagging.md ---
# Sandbagging clauses — pro- and anti-sandbagging

*Citation:* Delaware/Texas practice; *Akorn v. Fresenius* (Del. Ch. 2018) (dicta); ABA Private Target Deal Points Study  
*Status in this library:* in force

**Pro-sandbagging** clause: buyer may recover for breach of a representation even if it knew of the inaccuracy before signing/closing. **Anti-sandbagging**: buyer may not recover for breaches it knew of. Sellers who disclose a known issue (e.g., contractor classification) in diligence and then give a clean representation subject to a pro-sandbagging clause have effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue. The seller's protection is either (i) an anti-sandbagging clause, (ii) a disclosure schedule exception to the representation, or (iii) a special indemnity with a negotiated cap — not a clean rep.

--- tx_noncompete_sale_of_business.md ---
# Texas — non-competes ancillary to the sale of a business

*Citation:* Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §15.50; *Marsh USA v. Cook*, 354 S.W.3d 764 (Tex. 2011); sale-of-business cases  
*Status in this library:* in force

Covenants ancillary to the sale of a business are reviewed more leniently than employment covenants but must still be reasonable in time, area and scope; courts reform unreasonable covenants (§15.51(c)). Seven years / 500 miles for a local custom-cabinetry shop is likely overbroad as to both; 3–5 years within the trade area is typical. Reformation risk means the buyer, not the seller, should care — but an overbroad covenant allocated $400k of price (see tax engagement) invites IRS scrutiny of the allocation as well.

--- warn_act.md ---
# WARN Act thresholds

*Citation:* 29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1); 20 C.F.R. §639.3  
*Status in this library:* in force

WARN applies to employers with **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and to plant closings or mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site. A 14-employee business is **not** a covered employer; no WARN notice is required even if the buyer does not hire everyone. (Texas has no mini-WARN statute.)

--- worker_classification_tx_irs.md ---
# Worker classification — IRS common-law test; Texas Workforce Commission; successor exposure

*Citation:* IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41 (20 factors); Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; IRC §3509; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134  
*Status in this library:* in force

Individuals who work exclusively for one business, on its schedule, with its tools and vehicles, paid hourly, for years, are employees under the common-law control test regardless of the label. Exposure: employer FICA/FUTA (§3509 reduced rates if non-willful), state unemployment tax, overtime under the FLSA (hourly, >40 hrs), benefits eligibility, workers' comp. In an **asset sale**, the buyer generally does not inherit the seller's pre-closing payroll-tax liabilities, but may inherit **FLSA liability as a successor** where there is substantial continuity, and will have to reclassify going forward — which is why buyers price it and demand indemnity.

Now I have all the facts assembled. Let me check if there are any other documents — the seller's email says "I read the first 3 pages," and there's also a reference to a "tax matter" in the non-compete library file ("a covenant that is too broad with $400k of the purchase price allocated to it (see tax matter)"). Hmm, "tax matter" — is that a separate document? I don't see one. The library's tx_noncompete file states "an overly broad covenant with $400k of the purchase price allocated to it (see tax matter)." In our workspace, there is no allocation document other than the APA's earnout cap of $400k… Actually §8.2 is a non-compete, and the APA excerpt has no reference to a purchase price allocation. The $400k in the APA is the earnout cap. The reference to "tax matter" may be an intentional dangling reference (something not in the file) — I should not fabricate facts. Record the absence of a purchase price allocation as a missing fact / open question.

OK, let me plan the full engagement.

Key facts:
- Seller: Brightline Cabinetry LLC (Austin, Texas), Ray Brightline. 2025 revenue $4.6M; EBITDA $740k (seller-prepared, with add-backs).
- Buyer: Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC.
- Price: Purchase price not stated in APA excerpt! Escrow is $310,000 (10%), so purchase price is implied to be $3.1M. Confirm: $310,000 = 10% of purchase price → PP = $3.1M. Cap is 10% of PP = $310k.
- Earnout: 40% of EBITDA exceeding $700k over the 12 months post-closing, capped at $400k. So to get max earnout, EBITDA needs to exceed $700k + $1M = $1.7M. Given 2025 EBITDA is $740k (even adjusted), that's a huge stretch — 40% × (EBITDA − 700k) = 400k → EBITDA − 700k = 1M → EBITDA = 1.7M, more than double current. Effectively near-impossible earnout. Also "EBITDA as determined by Buyer under Buyer's accounting policies" — classic zero-out risk per the earnout library.

Arithmetic worth showing:
- Escrow $310k = 10% → implied PP $3.1M.
- Cap = 10% of PP = $310k.
- Basket: deductible $75k — is that above or below market? The ABA survey is the citation, but the library summary doesn't indicate basket %. Deductible vs. tipping is explained. $75k against $3.1M is about 2.4% — reasonable as market, but deductible favors seller. OK, keep.
- Earnout threshold: $400k cap requires TTM EBITDA of $1.7M; current is $740k → required growth = (1,700−700)/(740−700) = 25× the excess over current threshold. Or EBITDA needs to grow by about 130% ($740k→$1.7M). Effectively unattainable → the earnout is illusory value; the buyer is paying at most $3.1M… Wait, the purchase price amount isn't stated other than through escrow. Should flag as an assumption.

- Worker classification: 9 "1099 installers," dedicated, using Brightline tools/trucks, daily-scheduled by the foreman, hourly $34–41/hr, avg 3.4 years, total 2025 payments $612k. Under Rev. Rul. 87-41 20-factor / common-law control test → clearly employees. Exposure: employer share of FICA (Social Security 6.2% + Medicare 1.45% = 7.65%) and FUTA on 2025 wages $612k; IRC §3509 reduced rate for non-intentional misclassification: §3509(a) is 1.5% of wages for income tax withholding, 20% of employee FICA share? Actually §3509(a): if the payor hasn't intentionally disregarded the obligation, liable for (1) 1.5% of wages for income tax withholding, (2) 20% of the employer FICA amount (§3111 taxes). If intentional disregard: 2% and 100%. Should I calculate this? The contract requires showing arithmetic on numbers. I can compute an illustrative exposure using §3509(a) rates: 1.5% of $612k = $9,180 income tax withholding; 20% of employer FICA: 7.65% × 612,000 = $46,818; × 20% = $9,363.60. Total ~ $18,543.60 per year (federal, §3509(a) rate). Plus FUTA and SUTA. But do I know the §3509 rates from the library? The library cites IRC §3509 but doesn't list rates. Hmm. Working rule: "If a law you think you know isn't in the library, don't cite it — say so explicitly and label it unverified." The §3509 rates (1.5%, 20%) are my recollection, not in the library. I can present the calculation but label the rate source as unverified. Similarly FICA 7.65% — well known but not in the library. I should label these clearly as unverified multipliers and note that the statute cited in the library (IRC §3509) provides the reduced-rate mechanism but the library doesn't reproduce the rates.

Also multi-year exposure: 3.4-year average tenure but the statute of limitations on employment tax… not in the library. Keep as an illustration for one year and note that multi-year exposure is unknown.

Successor: In the asset sale, buyer generally doesn't assume pre-closing payroll taxes but may inherit FLSA successor liability given continuity and must reclassify going forward — per worker_classification library. So buyer will care: 9 people going forward as W-2, overtime exposure (hourly >40 hrs). Also buyer wants a 4.12 carve-out to full price cap — per baskets_caps library, carving a specific operational rep (worker classification is called out by name!) to a full price cap is off-market: should resist or replace with a sized special indemnity.

- Schedule 3.3 / consents: Hensley Homes MSA = 38% of revenue, §18 has a full anti-assignment provision that includes "sale of assets," sole discretion consent, attempted assignment void. Per SQL Solutions / anti-assignment library, that means transfer without consent is void = breach. So Buyer's "Schedule 3.3: None" is plainly wrong. Hensley consent is a gating condition — consent leverage: sole discretion means they can renegotiate price. 38% of revenue = 0.38 × $4.6M = $1.748M of revenue at risk. Cascade: assignment allowed with notice to substantially-all-asset successor — confirm asset sale qualifies as "successor to substantially all assets"; notice is required, so not literally "no required consents" but low risk; notice-based. Shop lease §22 needs landlord consent, not to be unreasonably withheld — need consent; schedule should include. Permits: non-transferable, must re-apply 30–60 days — timing item, and possibly an operational issue (can they operate without the spray booth?). 22 residential contracts silent on assignment — generally assignable (Restatement §317) unless personal services; risk is low; flag.

- WARN: 14 W-2 employees + 9 misclassified → even with reclassification, ~23; below 100-employee threshold; also layoffs are 50+ at a single site. So no WARN. Per library can confirm to buyer counsel: not a covered employer (14–23 < 100). Caution: even if reclassified installers are counted, total is 23 < 100. So confirmation OK.

- Sandbagging: 7.4(c) is pro-sandbagging ("Buyer's right shall not be affected by knowledge"). We know of the misclassification (it's in the data room, and I told the buyer). Per sandbagging library: if we disclose a known issue, give a clean 4.12 rep, and have a pro-sandbagging clause → we've agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue. Position on 7.4(c): seller should push for anti-sandbagging OR schedule exception on 4.12 OR a sized special indemnity instead of clean rep. Given the buyer already knows, pro-sandbagging + clean 4.12 rep + full price cap (7.4(b)) = up to $3.1M of exposure for a known, disclosed issue. This is the biggest trap.

- Survival: 4.12 + tax reps: SOL + 60 days; general 18 months — fine/standard per baskets_caps (12–24 months general).

- 8.2 Non-compete: 7 years / 500 miles from Austin for a local custom cabinetry shop — probably overly broad per §15.50 / Marsh USA; library says 3–5 years within the trading area is standard. Ray says "sign anything, I'm retiring" — but note: over-broad covenant → reformation risk (buyer's problem primarily), but library flags: over-broad covenant with $400k allocated to it invites IRS scrutiny of the allocation. Note: APA excerpt has no purchase price allocation; $400k is the earnout cap. The reference to "tax matter" isn't in our file. What Ray cares about: scope of the non-compete — "engaged in competition in the custom cabinetry business within 500 miles" — does consulting/selling to the industry count? As a retiree, he wants narrow scope; also consider: buyer can't enforce a void covenant anyway; reformation under §15.51(c). As seller's counsel: shorten to 3 years, Austin metro trading area (e.g., Travis County + adjacent counties), and clarify that passive investments are OK; also, don't sign "anything" because a non-compete that's too broad still gets partially enforced after reformation, and Ray might want to work at a competitor? He's retiring but — "retiring" can change. Recommend reasonable terms; consistent with library: courts reform, so buyer should care; but seller should not give an over-broad covenant because it constrains him and the price allocation issue (if any) invites IRS scrutiny.

- Earnout 2.4: "EBITDA as determined by Buyer under Buyer's accounting policies" → per earnout library, buyer can zero it out. Also threshold $700k vs. reported EBITDA $740k includes add-backs (owner comp $180k, litigation $42k) — under buyer's policies, the add-backs likely disappear → baseline EBITDA under buyer's accounting is $740k − $222k = $518k, well below threshold → earnout likely $0 even if business performs. Also required growth math: max payout requires $1.7M (need to show: 40% × (E − 700,000) = 400,000 → E = 1,700,000). 130% growth from 740k. Proposed fix: define EBITDA consistently with seller's historical practice/GAAP, exclude buyer overhead allocations / integration costs, covenant not to act with intent to frustrate earnout, information/audit rights, independent accountant, acceleration on sale. Also consider lowering the threshold, or noting the earnout is illusory in price negotiation: if the earnout is illusory, Ray should push cash at closing — price point.

- Escrow 9.3: $310k (10%) for 18 months vs. cap 10% ($310k) — escrow matches cap, but 4.12 carve-out cap = full price ($3.1M) means exposure beyond escrow; escrow is only 18 months but 4.12 survives SOL + 60 days — buyer can sue beyond escrow. Not strictly a redline fix in 9.3, but should tie: either cap 4.12 or size a special indemnity and backstop with escrow.

- Hardaway dispute $9,800 and warranty $23,000: below basket $75k — deductible basket means Ray pays only above $75k. However, warranty items could become rep breaches (no rep on 3.2 warranty given in excerpt). Note as diligence findings: small; consider disclosure.

- Data room financials: EBITDA $740k seller-prepared with add-backs; buyer may use different numbers in rep (e.g., rep on financials) but not in the excerpt. Earnout interaction already covered.

- 3.1 "Assigned Contracts listed on Schedule 3.1(c)" — need Hensley on it and consent obtained before closing; also Cascade's notice requirement.

APA redline target sections: 2.4, 3.3, 4.12, 7.4(a)-(c), 8.2, 9.3. Need keep/change decision + replacement text + reason for each.

Drafts:

2.4 — change. Replace: EBITDA means EBITDA of the business computed under GAAP consistently applied consistent with Seller's historical accounting practices set forth in Exhibit A (to include add-backs for owner comp at a market level and one-time expenses)… exclude: allocations of Buyer overhead, management fees, integration/transaction costs, purchase-accounting adjustments, non-cash charges; Buyer will operate the business in the ordinary course and will not act with the primary purpose of avoiding the earnout; access to books monthly; dispute resolution by independent accounting firm binding on both; accelerate on buyer's sale of business / failure to pay. Also change the threshold: given max $400k requires 130% EBITDA growth, negotiate threshold down (e.g., starting at $740k) or push price to cash side. Also pay earnout security via escrow or note.

3.3 — change: Schedule 3.3 to include: (i) Hensley Homes MSA §18 consent (sole discretion; without consent, assignment void), (ii) Cascade notice (permissive but required), (iii) landlord consent for shop lease §22 (not unreasonably withheld). Make Hensley consent a closing condition rather than "commercially reasonable efforts" — but caution: seller wouldn't want a condition he can't satisfy? Actually seller wants certainty; buyer wants a condition. As seller's counsel: "commercially reasonable efforts" is acceptable for the seller, but the schedule must list them (not "None"), and reps must be qualified by the schedule; and allocate: if Hensley refuses, buyer may walk — the price risk is on us. Recommend: list consents; define "Required Consents"; no rep that no consent is needed other than scheduled; consider making Hensley a condition to Buyer's obligation (buyer will push for this) — but seller should resist an open-ended walk right and instead set an outside date and a price adjustment if Hensley leaves. Keep the response measured.

4.12 — change: qualify with disclosure schedule: schedule exception for the 9 installers currently paid on 1099 basis; reframe: "Except as set forth in Schedule 4.12, Seller has properly classified…" plus add knowledge / law qualifiers; and address buyer's real concern by offering a specific, sized special indemnity for pre-closing employment taxes for the 1099 installers, with a cap (say 5–10% of price) and pre-closing-only scope, buyer responsible for classification post-closing. Alternative is to give the rep as-is knowing it's false — bad move.

7.4(a) — keep the deductible basket (favorable to seller); $75k ≈ 2.4% of implied $3.1M price — roughly market per ABA (library notes deductible vs. tipping but no basket %; call market-standard claim unverified? The library states market as: cap ~10% of price for general reps, fundamental reps + tax to price, survival 12–24 mos. Basket % isn't in library. I'll say deductible structure is favorable to seller and keep; the amount is roughly 2.4% of implied price — note that ABA survey doesn't specify in our library).

7.4(b) — change: carve-out of 4.12 from Cap to full price is off-market per baskets_caps ("carving a specific operational rep (e.g., worker classification) to full price cap is off-market and should be resisted or replaced with sized special indemnity"). Change: 4.12 to be subject to Cap, or replaced with a sized special indemnity for pre-closing worker classification / employment taxes, e.g., cap $150k–$310k (escrow as backstop). Compute exposure to size: illustrative 2025 federal employment tax exposure ~ $18.5k/yr at §3509(a) rate (label rates unverified) × number of open years + FUTA/SUTA + FLSA OT. Suggest special indemnity cap at, e.g., $150,000 (about 5% of price), backed by escrow.

7.4(c) — change: pro-sandbagging → anti-sandbagging: "Buyer shall not be entitled to indemnification for Losses arising from any breach of any representation that Buyer knew was inaccurate prior to signing (from Seller disclosure in the Data Room or otherwise)…" Position per sandbagging library. But note interplay: since we give a scheduled exception on 4.12, the sandbagging point is less critical; still prefer anti-sandbagging; if we can't get either, the buyer can already recover for a disclosed issue.

8.2 — change: 7 yrs / 500 miles probably overbroad per §15.50/Marsh (library); 3–5 yrs in trading area is standard. Ray is retiring but still: shorten to 3 years (maybe 5), geographic scope to Travis + adjacent counties, clarify that passive <1% stock is OK, and severability/reformation clause. Reason: enforceability and IRS allocation angle (library notes).

9.3 — keep amount / structure but adjust: $310k matches general cap of 10%; if we replace 4.12 carve-out with a sized special indemnity, escrow backstops it; consider splitting escrow into two tranches (a general 18 mo + a 4.12 tax tranche) and releasing the general escrow at 18 months; also ensure escrow is the sole source of recovery for general reps to avoid judgment risk. Or keep with note.

Reply to buyer's counsel:
- Schedule 3.3: not "None" — Hensley consent required (sole discretion; void if not obtained); Cascade notice; landlord consent. Ask them to update the schedule; will start the Hensley process but won't guarantee.
- WARN: confirm not a covered employer — 14 W-2 + 9 long-term 1099 (not counted) = 23; below 100; no plant closing / mass layoff of 50+ planned; Texas has no mini-WARN (per library). Caveat: confirmation based on current headcount; buyer's own post-close actions might implicate WARN but not seller.
- Position on 7.4(c): as drafted, pro-sandbagging + clean 4.12 + uncapped 4.12 cap = seller indemnifying for an issue buyer already knows about, up to full price. Our position: schedule exception on 4.12 and either anti-sandbagging on 7.4(c) or a sized special indemnity; if buyer wants pro-sandbagging, then the price must reflect an open, known issue — that's a price argument.

Note to Ray: three things that will bite you later:
1. Worker classification (9 installers) — clean 4.12 rep + uncapped + long survival + pro-sandbagging = up to $3.1M of exposure for something already disclosed; fix = schedule exception + sized special indemnity (or resist the carve-out).
2. Hensley Homes contract (38% of revenue) — buyer's Schedule 3.3 says no consents needed but §18 makes assignment without their consent void; if we sign the "no consents" rep, we're in breach; if Hensley balks, buyer walks or cuts price; fix = list consent, start talking to Hensley, control the message.
3. Earnout is nearly worthless as drafted — buyer controls EBITDA definition and baseline is below their policies ($740k includes $222k add-backs → buyer baseline ~$518k < threshold $700k); max $400k requires EBITDA $1.7M (130% growth); fix = define EBITDA, exclude their overhead, ordinary-course covenant, audit rights, or take cash instead.
Honorable mention: non-compete reasonableness (signing "anything" — 7 yrs / 500 miles is overbroad; if he does come back to work it binds him; reformation risk + IRS allocation scrutiny).

# APA redline — Brightline Cabinetry / Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC

Buyer's draft, key sections. Position is sell-side. **Assumption stated up front:** the excerpt does not state the Purchase Price; the escrow clause ($310,000 = "10%") implies **Purchase Price = $310,000 / 0.10 = $3,100,000**, so the 7.4(b) general cap = $310,000 and the §4.12 carve-out cap = $3,100,000. All percentages below use that figure; confirm (QUESTIONS.md Q1).

Citations are only to files in `library/INDEX.md`. Anything not in the library is labeled **UNVERIFIED**.

---

## §2.4 Earn-Out — **CHANGE**

**Problem (three layers):**
1. "EBITDA ... as determined by Buyer ... in accordance with Buyer's accounting policies" — the classic zero-out device. Buyer can allocate overhead, management fees, integration costs and purchase-accounting adjustments against the Business and pay nothing. See `library/earnout_definitions.md` (*Lazard Technology Partners v. Qinetiq*, 114 A.3d 193 (Del. 2015)).
2. The threshold is unreachable as drafted. Max payout requires 40% × (EBITDA − $700,000) = $400,000 → EBITDA = $700,000 + $400,000/0.40 = **$1,700,000**, vs. reported 2025 EBITDA of $740,000 — growth of ($1,700,000 − $740,000)/$740,000 = **129.7%**. Even if $740,000 were accepted unchanged, the payout is 0.40 × ($740,000 − $700,000) = **$16,000**.
3. The $740,000 itself is seller-prepared with $222,000 of add-backs (owner salary $180,000 + legal $42,000). Under any buyer policy that drops add-backs, run-rate EBITDA = $740,000 − $222,000 = **$518,000** — **$182,000 below the threshold**, so the earn-out is **$0** before Buyer allocates a dollar of overhead.

**Replacement language:**

> 2.4 Earn-Out. In addition to the Closing Payment, Buyer shall pay Seller an amount equal to 40% of the amount by which Adjusted EBITDA of the Business for the twelve (12) months following Closing exceeds $[518,000 / to be negotiated], up to a maximum of $400,000. "Adjusted EBITDA" means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of the Business, determined in accordance with GAAP consistently applied on a basis consistent with Seller's historical accounting practices as exhibited in Exhibit 2.4, and excluding: (i) any allocation of Buyer or Buyer-affiliate overhead, management fees, shared-service charges, or corporate costs to the Business; (ii) any transaction, integration, restructuring or purchase-accounting adjustment (including step-up depreciation/amortization) costs of Buyer; and (iii) [owner-salary and the identified one-time legal add-backs]. From and after the Closing, Buyer shall (x) operate the Business in the ordinary course consistent with past practice, (y) not take any action with the primary purpose of avoiding or reducing the Earn-Out, and (z) provide Seller monthly interim financial statements for the Business and audit rights on reasonable notice. Disputes under this Section shall be resolved by a mutually agreed independent accounting firm acting as expert, whose determination is binding, with costs allocated to the losing side. Upon a sale by Buyer of the Business or its relevant assets, the maximum Earn-Out amount becomes immediately due and payable. The Earn-Out shall be secured by [escrow/holdback note].

**Why:** `library/earnout_definitions.md` prescribes exactly this seller-protection set. Also tell Ray the commercial truth: as drafted this earn-out is worth approximately zero, so he should negotiate more closing cash rather than trade on the headline $400,000. If Buyer keeps a high threshold, the number alone (129.7% EBITDA growth required) is the argument.

---

## §3.3 Required Consents (and Schedule 3.3) — **CHANGE**

**Problem:** Schedule 3.3 says **"None."** That is false, and it is the most dangerous single word in the draft (see also the Schedule 3.3 answer in `reply_to_buyer_counsel.md`):
- **Hensley Homes MSA** (data room §1.1, 38% of revenue = 0.38 × $4.6M = **$1,748,000/yr**): §18 bars assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" without prior written consent "withheld in its sole discretion," and makes any purported assignment **void**. Per `library/anti_assignment_change_of_control.md` (*SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) §§317, 322), such a clause is enforced according to its terms — the asset sale transfers this contract only with consent, and transferring without it is a breach and void. "Sole discretion" gives Hensley renegotiation leverage.
- **Cascade Builders** (data room §1.2, 11% = $506,000/yr): permitted to a successor to substantially all assets **upon notice** — still a required notice; APA 3.1 (all assets) should satisfy the "substantially all" condition.
- **Shop lease** (data room §3.1): §22 landlord consent, not unreasonably withheld.

**Replacement language:**

> 3.3 Required Consents. Schedule 3.3 lists each consent or notice required under the Assigned Contracts in connection with the transactions contemplated hereby, and Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain such consents (or deliver such notices) prior to Closing. No representation or warranty in this Agreement shall be deemed breached, and no closing condition shall fail, solely by reason of the absence of any consent not expressly listed on Schedule 3.3 or by reason of the failure to obtain a listed consent, provided Seller has used such commercially reasonable efforts. [Negotiated bracket: if the Hensley consent is not obtained by the Outside Date, Buyer's sole remedy shall be [a purchase-price reduction equal to $[x] / termination], and Seller shall not be obligated to accept any modification of the Hensley MSA as a condition to consent.]

**Replacement Schedule 3.3:**

> Schedule 3.3 — Required Consents and Notices: (1) Hensley Homes — written consent to assignment of the Master Supply Agreement (§18) [approach to begin on signing]; (2) landlord at 7700 Burleson Rd — written consent to lease assignment (lease §22, not to be unreasonably withheld); (3) Cascade Builders — written notice of assignment to successor to substantially all assets (§ per framework agreement).

**Why:** keep "commercially reasonable efforts" (Seller can't guarantee Hensley's yes), but the schedule must be truthful or Ray signs a false rep on day one; and the Hensley consequence branch (walk vs. price cut) must be negotiated now, not after Hensley smells leverage.

---

## §4.12 Employees and Contractors — **CHANGE**

**Problem:** The rep as drafted ("all individuals ... properly classified ... and Seller has withheld and paid all required taxes") is **false at signing** — nine installers paid on 1099 work exclusively for Brightline, on its schedule, with its trucks and tools, hourly, averaging 3.4 years (data room §2.2). Under the common-law control test they are employees regardless of label (`library/worker_classification_tx_irs.md`: IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41; Treas. Reg. §31.3121(d)-1; IRC §3509; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134). A clean rep on a known, disclosed problem, combined with pro-sandbagging 7.4(c) and the full-price carve-out in 7.4(b), is exactly the trap described in `library/sandbagging.md`.

**Replacement language:**

> 4.12 Employees and Contractors. Except as set forth on Schedule 4.12 (identifying nine individuals currently compensated on Form 1099 as installers and the 2025 amounts paid), Seller has properly classified all individuals providing services to the Business as employees or independent contractors under applicable law, and Seller has withheld and paid all required taxes with respect to all such individuals, except to the extent arising from the classification disclosed on Schedule 4.12. Buyer acknowledges the disclosures on Schedule 4.12 and agrees that matters so disclosed shall be addressed exclusively under Section 7.5 (Worker Classification Special Indemnity) and shall not constitute a breach of this Section 4.12.

**Why:** this is the load-bearing fix. It converts a rep that Ray would breach on day one into (a) a disclosure and (b) a **sized, escrow-backed special indemnity** (see 7.4(b)). `library/sandbagging.md`: the seller's protections are an anti-sandbagging clause, a disclosure-schedule exception, or a special indemnity with a negotiated cap — *not a clean rep*. Ray's belief that "1099 forever, everyone does it" is legally irrelevant under the control test — do not litigate this belief into the rep.

# Reply to buyer's counsel (J. Whitaker, Lone Star Millwork Holdings LLC)

Re: Brightline Cabinetry asset sale — Schedule 3.3, WARN, and our position on APA 7.4(c)
Counsel: [Seller's counsel] for Brightline Cabinetry LLC and Ray Brightline

Mr. Whitaker — responses to the three points in your cover email, and one issue you did not raise that we will not sign around.

## 1. Schedule 3.3 is not "None" — three items must be listed

Your draft states there are no consent issues. The data room shows otherwise:

1. **Hensley Homes Master Supply Agreement (data room §1.1; 38% of revenue).** Section 18 prohibits assignment "by operation of law, merger, sale of assets, change of control or otherwise" without Hensley's prior written consent, which it "may ... withhold in its sole discretion," and provides that "any purported assignment in violation of this Section is void." A clause of exactly this type is enforced as written — transferring the agreement without consent is a breach and the transfer is void (*SQL Solutions v. Oracle*, 1991 WL 626458 (N.D. Cal.); Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§317, 322, per our reference set). This is a real closing item, not a formality. Our client will begin the consent approach promptly and use commercially reasonable efforts; neither party should pretend the outcome is guaranteed while consent may be "withheld in sole discretion."
2. **Cascade Builders framework agreement (data room §1.2; 11% of revenue).** Assignment is permitted to a successor to substantially all assets **upon notice**. Your 3.1 transfers all assets of the Business, so the condition should be satisfied — but the notice must actually be given, so this belongs on Schedule 3.3 as a notice item.
3. **Shop lease, 7700 Burleson Rd (data room §3.1; lease §22).** Landlord consent required, not to be unreasonably withheld. We expect no difficulty but it is a required consent.

Please repopulate Schedule 3.3 accordingly. We will also require that the consents representation be qualified by the schedule — our client cannot sign a "no other consents required" rep that the data room itself contradicts. The consequences if Hensley declines (price adjustment vs. termination right, with an outside date) should be negotiated in the document now; we will not accept "commercially reasonable efforts" backed by a false schedule.

Related and on timing only: the City of Austin spray-booth permit (data room §4.1) is issued to the LLC and is non-transferable; the new owner must reapply (stated 30–60 days). We propose a covenant that Buyer file its reapplication before Closing so there is no operational gap; Seller will cooperate with the underlying compliance file.

## 2. WARN — confirmed, no notice obligation on Seller

Based on the data room census (data room §2.1–2.2): 14 W-2 employees (7 shop, 4 installers, 3 office) and 9 long-tenure installers currently paid on Form 1099. Even counting every worker as an employee, headcount is 23.

WARN applies to employers of **100 or more employees** (excluding part-time) and to plant closings or mass layoffs affecting 50+ employees at a single site (29 U.S.C. §2101(a)(1); 20 C.F.R. §639.3). Brightline is not a covered employer, and Texas has no mini-WARN statute. **No WARN notice is required of Seller**, including if Buyer elects not to hire every installer at Closing. Two cautions, both for your side: (i) our confirmation is as of today's census and addresses Seller's obligations only — Buyer's post-closing staffing decisions are Buyer's matter; and (ii) do not read this answer as agreement with anything in §4.12; headcount is below WARN thresholds *whatever* the classification answer is.

## 3. Our position on 7.4(c) (sandbagging) — and the section it multiplies

Your draft pairs three provisions: (a) a clean §4.12 classification rep; (b) a 7.4(b) carve-out raising §4.12 to a cap equal to the **entire Purchase Price**; and (c) a pro-sandbagging clause preserving Buyer's claims "regardless of knowledge ... before or after execution." You have the classification facts from the data room. Putting the three together, you are asking our client to indemnify you, up to the full price, for an issue you already know about, surviving to the statute of limitations, with escrow at 10%. That is not a "knowledge" tweak — it is the deal's largest risk transfer, and the characterization as market-standard is half right: pro-sandbagging is one of two standard positions, and it is the buyer-favorable one (ABA Private Target Deal Points Study practice materials in our reference set). A seller who discloses a known issue, gives a clean rep, and accepts pro-sandbagging has effectively agreed to indemnify for the disclosed issue.

Our position:

- **§4.12**: qualified by a disclosure schedule identifying the nine 1099 installers and the 2025 amounts. Under the common-law control test (IRS Rev. Rul. 87-41; Tex. Lab. Code §201.041; 40 TAC §815.134), an unqualified rep would simply be false, and we will not negotiate as though it could be true.

# Note to Ray Brightline — what could cost you money after closing

Ray — you asked what bites you later. Three things, in order of how much they can cost you. Numbers shown so you can check them. (One assumption: the draft doesn't state the price; the escrow says "$310,000 (10%)", so the price reads as **$310,000 ÷ 0.10 = $3,100,000**. Tell me if that's wrong — several numbers below move with it.)

## 1. The nine "1099 installers" — the buyer already knows, and the draft makes it YOUR problem, uncapped

They work only for you, show up on the foreman's daily schedule, drive your trucks, use your tools, get paid hourly ($34–41/hr), and average 3.4 years each. Under the IRS's control test that's employment — "everyone in the industry does it" is not a defense, and the data room shows these facts to the buyer in black and white. 2025 payments to them: $612,000 (about $68,000 each).

Now look at what the buyer's draft does with that:

- §4.12 asks you to *represent* everyone is properly classified. You'd be signing a false statement on day one.
- §7.4(b) says breaches of that one rep are capped not at the usual 10% but at the **whole price — $3,100,000** — and the survival runs to the tax statute of limitations, years past closing.
- §7.4(c) (the "knowledge" clause) says the buyer can claim **even for problems it already knew about**. The buyer has your data room. You disclose the issue, then indemnify them for it, uncapped.

Rough size of the actual tax problem (federal, one year, using the reduced non-willful rates in IRC §3509 — the library cites the statute but not its percentages, so treat the rates as estimates): 1.5% × $612,000 = $9,180, plus 20% of employer FICA (7.65% × $612,000 = $46,818) = $9,364 — about **$18,500/yr**, so call it **$75,000–$80,000 for four open years**, before state unemployment taxes and any overtime claims (the installers are hourly; if they worked 50-hour weeks, overtime adds up — tell me their hours). The buyer's own go-forward cost — putting nine people on payroll — is why they want you holding the bag for the past.

**The fix (already drafted in the redline):** put the nine on a disclosure schedule instead of lying in the rep, and offer a **special indemnity capped at $150,000**, held in the escrow, as the buyer's only remedy for this. The library-backed market rule is blunt: carving one operational rep like worker classification up to a full-price cap is off-market and should be resisted. Say no to the full-price carve-out, no to the clean rep, and no to the pro-knowledge clause unless the schedule fix is in.

## 2. Hensley Homes — 38% of your revenue, and their contract says the sale is void without their signature

Hensley is your biggest customer: 38% of $4.6M = **$1,748,000/yr**. Their Master Supply Agreement, §18, says you can't assign it "by ... sale of assets" without their written consent, they can say no "in its sole discretion", and a transfer without consent is **void**. The buyer's Schedule 3.3 says "None" — no consents needed. That's wrong, and signing that page plus the rep behind it means you personally start the deal in breach.

This is a process problem, not a deal-killer — but it has to be worked **now**, before signing: tell the buyer the truth (reply drafted), start the Hensley conversation this week, and decide in the contract what happens if Hensley tries to re-price or walk (a defined price cut or a termination right — not "we tried our best" with a false schedule behind it). Cascade Builders (11% = $506,000/yr) only needs *notice*; the shop lease needs landlord consent but the standard is "not unreasonably withheld."

## 3. The earn-out is nearly worth zero as written — don't trade real money for it

The draft pays 40% of next-year EBITDA over $700,000, max $400,000. Do the math:

- To collect the full $400,000, EBITDA must hit $700,000 + $400,000 ÷ 0.40 = **$1,700,000** — that's **129.7% above** your reported $740,000. Nobody doubles EBITDA in a year under new owners.
- At your current run-rate, the payout is 40% × ($740,000 − $700,000) = **$16,000**. At best.
- Worse: your $740,000 counts on add-backs (your $180,000 salary + $42,000 legal). Under *buyer's* accounting policies — which is what the draft says EBITDA means — that's $740,000 − $222,000 = **$518,000**, which is **$182,000 under the threshold**: the earn-out pays **$0**, and the buyer controls the calculator. This exact trick (buyer allocates overhead and integration costs into "EBITDA as determined by Buyer") is the known pathology in the case law.

**The fix:** a real EBITDA definition (your historical practices, buyer overhead and integration costs excluded), ordinary-course operation, audit rights, an outside accountant judging disputes, acceleration if they flip the business — or, simpler, treat the earn-out as worth ~nothing and demand more cash at closing.

## Two smaller things that only bite if you're careless

- **"I'll sign whatever non-compete."** Don't. Seven years / 500 miles is more than a court would enforce for a shop like yours (Texas law: 3–5 years in your trade area is the typical enforceable range for a business sale, and a court will trim it, not delete it — meaning you'd still be bound). We've countered at 3 years, Travis County plus neighbors. If you ever consult, help a friend's shop, or hate retirement in year two, that page matters.
- **Small claims tail** (Hardaway $9,800 + warranty log $23,000 = $32,800): under the $75,000 deductible basket you'd pay nothing unless total claims cross $75,000 — keep the basket deductible and disclose these openly.

## Good news, free of charge

The buyer asked whether WARN notices are needed — no. With 14 W-2 employees (23 counting the installers), you're nowhere near the 100-employee threshold, and Texas has no mini-WARN. Confirming that costs you nothing and buys credibility for the fights that do matter.

**What I need from you to finish:** answers to the questions in QUESTIONS.md (price confirmation, the installers' hours, the Hensley relationship, any non-compete allocation in the deal papers). Then: do not sign anything until §§4.12, 7.4(b)-(c), 3.3/Schedule 3.3, 2.4 and 8.2 are redlined as proposed. Two weeks is workable only if the Hensley conversation starts this week.
